::: {.lead}
*Rooftop Rescue* goes live in two weeks. Salma needs a promo of 30 seconds
for the store page: the first thing that many players will see. Tariq has
two minutes of gameplay capture, the music of the game and the logo. "In
three seconds people decide if they keep watching," says Salma. In lectures
19–21 you learned video formats, the editor and the craft of cutting. In
this seminar each student **edits a promo**: you plan its parts, write a
shot list, cut it, and review it with a checklist. Every section ends with a
task, and at the end you have your own promo of a game.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary promo-clip hook shot-list pacing cut-on-action title-safe-area call-to-action export-preset >}}

## 22.1 The parts of a promo

A good promo is not a random set of nice shots: it has a structure
(@fig-structure).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 22.1 — Five parts of a 30-second promo"}
1. **Hook** (0–3 s): the most exciting shot first.
2. **The world** (≈ 3–9 s): where and who, with the title.
3. **Gameplay beats** (≈ 9–20 s): short shots (1–3 s) of what the player
   does, on the beat of the music.
4. **The big moment** (≈ 20–25 s): the best surprise or emotion.
5. **Logo and call to action** (last ≈ 5 s): the name and what to do, such
   as "Play free now".

No menus, loading screens or long walks: only moments that make people want
to play.
:::

![A 30-second promo in five parts.](images/promo-structure.png){#fig-structure width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 22.1 — The plan of the Rooftop Rescue promo"}
1. Hook: the wave hits the roof and Nour jumps (2.5 s).
2. The world: the flooded town, with the title.
3. Beats: rowing in the rain, the net catches Pasha, three short level shots,
   the giant wave.
4. Big moment: Pasha is safe on the roof, Nour smiles.
5. End: the logo and "Play free now", while the music ends.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Opening with the logo and the studio name for 5 seconds. Many viewers leave
before the first shot of the game. The logo belongs at the end.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Choose your game"}
Choose a game you can record (your own project, a free game, or the clips of
Timeline Lab). Write one line for each of the five parts.

*Your result:* a plan of five lines.
:::

## 22.2 From the capture to a shot list

Before you cut, choose the shots and write them down (@fig-shotlist).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 22.2 — Shot list"}
A **shot list** gives each shot its number, its start time in the promo,
what it shows, its length, and a note (for example "cut on action", "title
in", "on the beat"). Mark the best moments in the capture first, then
choose. Shots that do not serve one of the five parts stay out.
:::

![A shot list for the Rooftop Rescue promo.](images/shot-list.png){#fig-shotlist width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 22.2 — Choosing the shots"}
1. Tariq watches the two-minute capture and marks 14 good moments.
2. The menu, the loading screen and a slow walk on the roof are not used.
3. Nine shots are left; together with the logo they make 25–30 seconds.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/promo-builder.html" poster="sims/promo-builder.png" title="Promo Builder: 30 seconds of Rooftop Rescue" height="940" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Keeping a shot "because it took long to record". The viewer does not know
how hard a shot was; only the promo matters.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Your shot list"}
1. In **Promo Builder**, make all six checks green.
2. Write the shot list of your own promo (at least six shots) with times and
   notes.

*Your result:* a shot list.
:::

## 22.3 Cutting the promo

Now the plan becomes an edit (lectures 20 and 21).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 22.3 — Cutting rules for a promo"}
- Put the **music** on A1 first and mark its beats; cut on the beats.
- Use **cuts** and cuts on action; one **dip to black** before the logo.
- **Titles:** few words, real features ("Rescue cats in 30 levels"), inside
  the title safe area, at least 2 s on screen.
- **Call to action** at the end, with the name of the game.
- Use only music, pictures and fonts that you may use (lectures 23–26).
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 22.3 — Cutting on the beat"}
1. The music has a beat every 0.5 s: Tariq places markers on the beats.
2. The level shots are 1.5 s each: three beats per shot.
3. The giant wave comes with the loudest part of the music, the logo with the
   last chord.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Titles that promise what the game does not have ("Online multiplayer!" in a
single-player game). It is dishonest, players feel cheated, and stores can
reject a misleading listing.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Cut it"}
Cut your promo in the video editor: the music first, then the shots of your
shot list on the beats, one title, the logo and the call to action.

*Your result:* a first cut of your promo.
:::

## 22.4 Review and export

A last check catches the mistakes that the editor no longer sees
(@fig-check).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 22.4 — The review"}
Watch the promo three times: once as a player (Is it exciting? Do I know
the game?), once with the checklist, once on a phone. Then export it with
the settings of the target (lecture 19) and a clear file name with a
version.
:::

![The review checklist.](images/promo-check.png){#fig-check width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 22.4 — Version 2"}
1. On the phone, the call to action is cut off: Tariq moves it into the safe
   area.
2. The checklist shows a 6-second shot in the middle: it is cut to 3 s.
3. Export `rooftop-promo-v2.mp4`, H.264, 1920 × 1080, 30 fps, 28 s.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Reviewing only on the big monitor. Most players will see the promo on a
phone, often without sound: the pictures and titles must work alone too.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Review and export"}
Review your promo with the checklist and on a phone, fix two things, and
export it as `yourname-promo-v2.mp4`.

*Your result:* a promo file and two fixes.
:::

## Case study: Promo Judge

Six students show their promos: one opens with a 5-second logo, one is 55
seconds long for a social feed, one says "The best game ever!!!", one ends
without the name, one uses a famous song found online, and one cuts between
the beats. The Game challenge of the interactive lesson uses these promos.

## Further reading

Fullerton, *Game Design Workshop*, 4th ed., Chapter 15 (pitching and
promoting a game). Murch, *In the Blink of an Eye*, 2nd ed. (2001).

## Exercises

1. Name the five parts of a 30-second promo.
2. Why does the hook come first?
3. Which shots stay out of a promo?
4. What does a shot list contain?
5. How long are the shots of the gameplay beats?
6. Why put the music on the timeline first?
7. Give an honest title for a game feature.
8. What is a call to action?
9. Why review the promo on a phone?
10. Which settings do you choose for the export?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. Hook, the world, gameplay beats, the big moment, logo and call to action.
2. Viewers decide in about 3 seconds if they keep watching.
3. Menus, loading screens, slow and empty moments.
4. Number, start time, content, length and a note for each shot.
5. About 1–3 seconds.
6. To cut the shots on its beats.
7. For example "Rescue cats in 30 levels".
8. The end that tells viewers what to do, such as "Play free now".
9. Most viewers watch on phones, often without sound; text may be cut off.
10. The settings of the target, for example H.264 in MP4, 1920 × 1080,
    30 fps, and a clear file name with a version.
:::
